slides.title: Purpose
bullets: Sputum is the pathological discharge of the airways brought up by coughing; a healthy person does not produce it.
The examination includes the physical and chemical properties of the sputum, its microscopic content and the bacteriological aspect.

In lower-respiratory-tract infections (bronchitis, pneumonia, lung abscess, lung tuberculosis) many patients bring up green or yellowish purulent sputum; in others there is little or none, so diagnosis should be done in a specialised laboratory.
Microscopy and staining of smears are in the protocol “Staining sputum smears by Gram and Ziehl–Neelsen”.

slides.title: Collecting the sputum
bullets: 1. Sputum is collected early in the morning, before eating and, if possible, before antimicrobial treatment starts; Aripova says to collect it outside the building.
2. First the patient rinses the mouth with water (Kurbonova: the teeth are also cleaned).
3. The patient takes a deep breath, holds it, coughs hard and spits the sputum into the container held to the lower lip.

slides.title: Collecting the sputum
bullets: 4. Container: sterile, degreased, free of disinfectant residue, wide-mouthed with a tight lid (Aripova: 50 mL or larger; Kurbonova: a sterile container).
5. Amount: Kurbonova considers 3–5 mL enough; Aripova says to repeat the collection if there is less than 2–5 mL.
6. A watery specimen, or one mixed with food or nasal mucus, is unsuitable — collection is repeated.

slides.title: Delivery and macroscopic inspection
bullets: 1. Kurbonova: the analysis is done within 2 hours of collection; until delivery the closed container is kept in a refrigerator.
2. Check that the details on the container match the request form; examine specimens one at a time.
3. Without opening the container assess the appearance and colour of the sputum; if the container is of dark glass, take every precaution when opening it.

slides.title: Delivery and macroscopic inspection
bullets: 4. Write the appearance and colour on the request form.

slides.title: Appearance, colour and character
rows: Acute bronchitis, pneumonia, congestion in the lungs, onset of an asthma attack
Pulmonary oedema, purulent lung disease (abscess, bronchiectasis, gangrene, tuberculosis)
Bloody sputum / breakdown of red cells — lobar pneumonia

slides.title: Appearance, colour and character
rows: Catarrhal inflammation / bronchitis, pneumonia, bronchiectasis, tuberculosis / purulent bronchitis, abscess, gangrene
Pulmonary oedema / lung infarct, tumours, lung injury

slides.title: Native microscopy: what is looked for
rows: Found in small numbers; more than 25 per field means the material is mixed with saliva
Comes from the pharynx, trachea and bronchi
Many — strong inflammation, mucopurulent or purulent sputum
Bronchial asthma, eosinophilic pneumonia, lung infestation with worms, lung infarct

slides.title: Native microscopy: what is looked for
rows: When a malignant tumour of the respiratory organs breaks down
Breakdown of lung tissue: tuberculosis, abscess, echinococcosis, lung tumours
Obstructive bronchial disease (asthma, obstructive bronchitis); Charcot–Leyden — asthma, eosinophilic infiltrates, lung worms
Fungal involvement of the bronchopulmonary system

slides.title: Sources of error and quality control
bullets: Many squamous epithelial cells mean saliva contamination: more than 25 per low-power (×100) field — a poor specimen; the best specimens have fewer than 10 squamous cells and more than 25 leukocytes per field. Interpret with care or ask for a repeat specimen.
A watery specimen, or one mixed with food or nasal mucus, is unsuitable.
Drugs (for example rifampicin) can change the colour of sputum.

A good specimen is essential for a reliable analysis; Aripova advises keeping in the laboratory a set of unstained smears made from positive sputum and checking each new batch of stain alongside every specimen.

slides.title: Safety
bullets: Any sputum is hazardous: it may be infected and contain tubercle bacilli.
Safe collection and handling of the material is done by an experienced member of staff; at the first collection the patient is watched by someone who knows the technique.
Work in protective clothing (gloves, gown, protective equipment).
Disinfect used containers, slides and instruments (according to the regulation in force).
